..
Issued at 421 AM CDT Sun Sep 13 2026

We are in zonal flow aloft as upper ridging has been pushed to the 
southern tier of the CONUS, while a cutoff low spins over the 
Pacific Northwest and broader cyclonic flow encompasses the rest of 
the northern CONUS thanks to another low near the Hudson Bay. A 
surface low sits in the eastern NM and west TX vicinity with its 
frontal boundary remaining stationary in southern KS early this 
morning. WAA north of the front has sustained scattered storms 
across much of the CWA despite the LLJ not being overly strong at 
around 25-30 kts. Storms may decrease in coverage through the 
morning as the jet weakens, but with the WAA regime staying in place 
through the day, am hesitant to buy into the CAM solutions that dry 
us out completely earlier in the day. It would seem reasonable to at 
least keep some isolated or widely scattered showery activity into 
the afternoon, so held onto low chance PoPs to account for that 
possibility. Outside of rain, the sfc boundary may lift north some 
today with clearing skies more likely to occur south of the front. 
However far north it manages to make it will determine how warm 
temperatures will get. For that reason, highs in the 80s are mostly 
confined to areas south of I-70 with locations north remaining in 
the 70s today. Later tonight, CAMs redevelop elevated convection 
along the instability gradient within the WAA regime, but vary in 
its eastward/westward placement. Some solutions keep all of this 
east into MO, while others include part of northeast KS. Most of 
this activity shouldn't be severe, but with effective shear around 
30 kts, that will be something to monitor.

On Monday, there is good agreement on the warm air surging north 
with breezy southerly winds. This brings a quick warm-up with highs 
in the 90s and heat indices near 100 degrees. Dry weather is 
expected in the warm sector, so the main focus for storms will be 
with the approach of the cold front in north central KS during the 
late afternoon and evening. Shear is modest around 25-30 kts, but 
inverted-V soundings indicate a potential wind threat if an updraft 
grows strong enough. The severe threat should diminish later in the 
evening and overnight as instability decreases.

As we get into Tuesday, this is where this system could become more 
impactful but there is still a fair amount of uncertainty. The cold 
front looks to slowly sag south through the day, and its location in 
the afternoon and evening will ultimately determine where the severe 
and hydro threats will be greatest. With clearer skies south of the 
front comes greater instability, and with slightly better shear and 
more instability compared to Monday, think Tuesday presents a 
slightly better severe weather setup with damaging wind and perhaps 
hail up to 1 inch as potential threats. The bigger concern with time 
is that storms may train over the same locations with storm motions 
being parallel to the front. This along with ensemble guidance 
showing Pwat near the 99th percentile indicates some concern for 
locally heavy rainfall amounts. NBM currently has a 40-80% 
probability of totals exceeding 2" by 12z Wednesday (mainly along 
and north of I-70), though it should be noted that this is only 
incorporating the coarser model guidance for now. Of the high-res 
models, only the 00z and 06z RRFS go out far enough, and for now 
they show a couple swaths of 2-4" indicating a more localized heavy 
rain threat. Once we get within range of more CAM guidance, we 
should get a better idea of the potential for any higher-end amounts 
that could be more concerning, and where the heavy rain axis might 
be.

The front may move around a little bit later in the week, but looks 
to stall somewhere in the region. Given the uncertainty in exactly 
where it will be each day Wednesday onward, temperature spreads 
remain large in the ensemble guidance and PoPs continue through the 
end of the week. In any case, warmer temperatures in the 80s 
(possibly around 90) can be expected south of the front with cooler 
temperatures in the 70s north, especially if clouds and rain linger. 
The placement of the front will also be key in determining where 
flooding concerns could grow, as multiple rounds of rain over the 
same locations would become a problem, but if later rounds go 
through areas less impacted earlier in the week, that would limit 
the risk. By next weekend, we finally get a strong enough shortwave 
in the area to push the front south with better agreement on cooler 
temperatures.
